entries.modern_form: PIE *bʰili-, *bʰilo- 'harmonious, fitting, good, friendly' (Watkins: bhilo- 'dear, familiar')
entries.note: Pokorny IEW 153-154 has the lemma exactly as Nourai names it: 'bhili-, bhilo- ‚ebenmäßig, angemessen, gut, freundlich‘', with Mir. bil 'good', Gaul. Bili- in names, OHG bila-/bili-, bil-lich, OE bile-wit, MHG unbil, NHG Unbilde. Walde-Pokorny II 185 and Mann (IEC 'bhilos (1) “good, fair, friendly, pleasant”') agree, and Watkins gives 'bhilo-. Dear, familiar.' So the root form, the language label 'Indo-European' and the gloss 'good, friendly, loving' are all correct. The chart's own NOTE, 'SYN:1110 claims this is an Anatolian word', is accurate and important: Buck p.1110 (16.27 LOVE) writes that Greek philos, 'in Hom. also “one's own”, this perh. the earliest sense and so fr. an Anatolian word represented by Lyd. bilis “one's own” (Kretschmer, IF 45.267 ff.)'. That doubt bears only on the Greek branch — i.e. on node #1, and through it on the whole page — not on the Germanic/Celtic root itself, which is secure. Beekes (2010) likewise rejects the IE etymology of philos. The page is otherwise a clean Greek-Latin-French-English fan with two Persian offshoots; the only real error is the misprint philo-anthôpos (node #19) and the Greek label on the modern coinage philo-armonica (node #8).
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *bʰili-/*bʰilo- «متناسب، شایسته، نیک، دوستانه»؛ پوکورنی در صفحات ۱۵۳–۱۵۴ همین مدخل را با همین نام و همین معنا آورده و والده–پوکورنی، مان و واتکینز نیز آن را تأیید می‌کنند؛ پس نام ریشه، برچسب زبانی و معنای آن در کتاب درست است. یادداشت خود نورایی («SYN:1110 آن را واژه‌ای آناتولیایی می‌داند») عیناً درست است: باک در صفحهٔ ۱۱۱۰ می‌نویسد که معنای کهن‌تر φίλος در هومر «از آنِ خود» است و شاید از لیدیایی bilis آمده باشد. این تردید تنها به شاخهٔ یونانی (گرهٔ ۱) مربوط است نه به خود ریشه. در سراسر صفحه تنها دو ایراد جدی هست: غلط چاپی philo-anthôpos و یونانی خواندن ساختهٔ جدید philo-armonica.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt (leaf with the printed page-number 154 immediately after it) s.v. 'bhili-, bhilo-': „bhili-, bhilo- ,ebenmaßig, angemessen, gut, freundlich‘“ — exactly Nourai's root name, language label and gloss. English Pokorny (POK_full.txt, 'Root / lemma: bʰili-, bʰilo-, Meaning: harmonious, friendly, Page(s): 153-154').

Quoted from the root's own NOTE. SYN.txt, printed page 1110 (the page numeral '1110' stands two lines above): 'Grk. φιλέω “love” (have affection for), φιλία “friendly love, friendship”, fr. φίλος “dear”, sb. “friend”, in Hom. also “one's own”, this perh. the earliest sense and so fr. an Anatolian word represented by Lyd. bilis “one's own”. Kretschmer, IF 45.267 ff.' — exactly what Nourai reports.

consulted.note: 'bhili-, bhilo- ‚ebenmäßig, angemessen, gut, freundlich‘. Mir. bil (*bhi-li-) ‚gut‘, gall. Bili- in PN Bili-catus, Bilicius usw., ahd. bila- ‚gütig‘ … ahd. bil-lich ‚geziemend‘ … mhd. unbilde … nhd. Unbilde.'

'bhilo- etwa „in gutem Sinne ebenmaßig, angemessen, gut, freundlich“. Vermutlich gr. φίλος „lieb, wert usw.“ … Ir. bil „gut“, gall. Bil- in vielen EN.' — Pokorny's direct forerunner (his own reference 'WP. II 185').
'bhilo-. Dear, familiar. Possible source of Greek philos, dear, loving (> philein, to love): -PHILE, -PHILIA, PHILO-, -PHILOUS, PHILTER; PAM. [Pok. bhili- 153.]'
'bhilos (1) “good, fair, friendly, pleasant”. WP II, 185  Myc. piro- (*philo-); Gk. phílos; OIr. bil (1) “fortunate” … MHG bil-lich, -liche “fair, fairness”.'
Buck prefers the Anatolian source for Greek φίλος and does not connect it with the Germanic/Celtic 'billig' family.

nodes.derivation: Greek φίλος 'dear, beloved', as a noun 'friend' (Homeric also 'one's own'), whence φιλέω 'I love' and φιλία 'friendship'; Nourai's gloss 'love' is loose — the word is an adjective/noun, 'love' is φιλία. The derivation from the root is the traditional one (*bʰil-o-s > φίλος with regular IE *bʰ > Gk. φ and thematic *-o-s > -ος, cognate with OIr. bil 'good', OHG bili-/billih 'fitting, fair', NHG billig, Unbill), and Mann even adds Mycenaean pi-ro- = *philo-. But Pokorny himself does NOT list φίλος among the descendants: on p.154 he only reports Kretschmer's rival view (IF 45.267 ff.) that it is an Asianic/Anatolian word matching Lydian bilis 'his own', with Loewe against. Watkins hedges ('Possible source of Greek philos'), Klein calls it 'of uncertain origin', and Beekes rejects the IE etymology altogether because the oldest sense is 'own, accompanying' rather than 'beloved', leaving the origin open. So the arrow is one accepted scholarly option, not consensus.
nodes.derivation_fa: «فیلوس» (φίλος) در یونانی باستان صفت است به معنی «عزیز، دوست‌داشتنی» و در کاربرد اسمی «دوست»؛ پس معنایی که نورایی آورده («love») دقیق نیست و معادل φιλία است. ریشه‌شناسی سنتی آن را از هندواروپایی آغازین *bʰil-o-s می‌گیرد (ب‌ میان‌دمیدهٔ هندواروپایی در یونانی به ف بدل می‌شود)، هم‌ریشه با ایرلندی میانه bil «خوب» و آلمانی بالای کهن billih. اما خود پوکورنی در صفحهٔ ۱۵۴ این واژه را جزء بازمانده‌های ریشه نیاورده و تنها نظر کرچمر را نقل کرده که آن را وام‌واژه‌ای آسیایی (لیدیایی bilis) می‌داند؛ بیکس نیز ریشهٔ هندواروپایی را رد می‌کند. بنابراین ادعای نورایی با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

The page Nourai cites therefore records the φίλος question but does NOT assert the derivation from bhili-; it presents the Anatolian alternative.

nodes.derivation: Greek φιλόσοφος 'lover of wisdom' = φίλος + σοφός 'wise, skilled' (a word Beekes calls of unknown origin), an ordinary Greek determinative compound with the linking vowel -o- of the first member; attested from Herodotus (1.30) and Heraclitus onward, and made a technical term by Plato, with the abstract φιλοσοφία. The formation is inner-Greek and uncontroversial.
nodes.derivation_fa: یونانی φιλόσοφος (philosophos) «دوستدار حکمت» ترکیبی است از philos «دوستدار» و sophos «دانا، فرزانه» با میانوند -o- که در ترکیب‌های یونانی معمول است. این واژه از هرودوت و هراکلیتوس به بعد گواهی شده و افلاطون آن را اصطلاح فلسفی کرد. ساخت واژه درون‌یونانی و بی‌چون‌و‌چرا است؛ ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1971.txt s.v. philosophy: 'fr. Gk. φιλοσοφία, “love of wisdom, philosophy”, fr. φιλόσοφος, “lover of wisdom, philosopher”.'
Watkins 1985 s.v. bhilo- lists PHILO- among the English reflexes of Greek philos; the compound philosophos is the standard example of the combining form.

consulted.note: 'philo-, before a vowel phil-, combining form meaning “loving, fond of, interested in”, as in philosopher.'
'philosophy, love of wisdom. (F.—L.—Gk.) … Gk. φιλοσοφία, love of … Gk. φιλόσοφος, loving know[ledge] … Gk. φίλος, fond of; σοφός, skilful.'

nodes.derivation: Arabic فَلْسَفَة falsafa 'philosophy' entered Arabic in the 3rd/9th-century translation movement, through Syriac ـfilosofā, and was re-analysed on the native quadriliteral pattern faʿlalah, producing a new consonantal root فلسف with the verb فَلْسَفَ / تَفَلْسَفَ and the agent noun فَيْلَسُوف faylasūf (pl. فَلاسِفة falāsifa). Nourai's arrow φιλόσοφος > falsafah is one of the two routes modern sources allow, but the direct model of the ABSTRACT noun is φιλοσοφία: Wiktionary gives 'from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία, either directly or through فَيْلَسُوف', the latter (< φιλόσοφος) being the form that actually matches Nourai's Greek etymon. Hence plausible rather than exact.
nodes.derivation_fa: عربی «فلسفه» در جنبش ترجمهٔ سدهٔ سوم هجری، بیشتر از راه سریانی، از یونانی philosophia وام گرفته شده و سپس بر وزن رباعی «فَعْلَلَة» بازتحلیل شده و ریشهٔ ساختگیٔ «ف‌ل‌س‌ف» پدید آورده است با فعل «تفلسف» و اسم فاعل «فیلسوف» (جمع: فلاسفه). نورایی پیکان را از philosophos کشیده است که درست‌تر منشأ «فیلسوف» است، نه «فلسفه»؛ از این‌رو ادعا با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

ref_check.note: TAD_pages.txt leaf 56 (0-based; printed page ≈ 51-53, the book's own numeral is not legible in the OCR): 'فلسفة — يوناني Philosophia معناه حب الحكمة ومنه تفلسف وفيلسوف' (OCR: 'فاسفة ل ونانى … معناه حب المكة ومنه تقليف وفيلسوف'). Al-Unaysi thus gives the Greek source and the derived تفلسف/فيلسوف, as Nourai claims; he names philosophia, not philosophos.

consulted.note: Klein has the Greek chain (φιλοσοφία < φιλόσοφος) but says nothing about the Arabic borrowing.

nodes.derivation: New Persian فلسفه falsafe 'philosophy' is a straight Arabic loan (Arabic فَلْسَفَة), taken over with the Arabic tāʾ marbūṭa written ـه and pronounced -e in Persian, current from the earliest Islamic-Persian philosophical prose onward. The box's extra forms belong to the same Arabic quadriliteral family: فیلسوف faylsūf/filsuf (Ar. فَيْلَسُوف < Gk. φιλόσοφος) and its broken plural فلاسفه falāsefe. Mo'in tags the headword [ع.] = Arabic, confirming the immediate donor language of the chart.
nodes.derivation_fa: «فلسفه» در فارسی نو وام‌واژهٔ مستقیم از عربی فَلْسَفَة است که تاء مربوطهٔ آن در فارسی به ـه نوشته و -e خوانده می‌شود؛ معین در فرهنگ فارسی آن را با نشانهٔ [ع.] می‌آورد: «(فَ لْ سَ فِ) [ع.] (اِ.) ۱- حکمت، دانشی که موضوع آن هستی و وجود است». واژه‌های افزودهٔ جعبه (فیلسوف، فلاسفه) نیز از همین ریشهٔ رباعی عربی‌اند. ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: The Mo'in entry was verified online (vajehyab.com/moein/فلسفه): '(فَ لْ سَ فِ) [ع.] (اِ.) ۱- حکمت، دانشی که موضوع آن هستی و وجود است. ۲- علت، دلیل' — the [ع.] tag is exactly Nourai's Arabic parent. The printed page number 2567 could not be checked: the online Mo'in has no pagination and the local MON_part1/2 files are the 2-volume Adena reprint.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node: Latin took φιλόσοφος/φιλοσοφία as philosophus, philosophia already in the Republican period (Cicero uses philosophia as a naturalised word and coins Latin equivalents for its terminology), with the regular transliteration Gk. φ > Lat. ph and Gk. -ος/-ία > Lat. -us/-ia. From Latin the word passed into all the Romance languages.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node: Old French filosofie / philosophie is attested from the 12th century, a learned borrowing from Latin philosophia with the Old French learned ending -ie for Latin -ia. English took the word from this Old French form (and partly re-latinised the spelling).

nodes.derivation: English philosophy is first attested c.1300 as philosophie 'knowledge, learning, scholarship', from Old French filosofie (12c.) and directly from Latin philosophia; Middle English shows many spellings (filozofie, phelosophie). The sense narrows to 'rational speculation' in the mid-14th c. and to 'the science of the most fundamental matters' by 1794.
nodes.derivation_fa: انگلیسی philosophy نخست در حدود ۱۳۰۰ میلادی به صورت philosophie به معنی «دانش و دانش‌وری» گواهی شده است، از فرانسهٔ کهن filosofie و مستقیماً از لاتینی philosophia. در انگلیسی میانه املاهای گوناگونی داشته و معنای فنی امروزی آن از سدهٔ هجدهم پدید آمده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Two of the three are genuine Greek compounds: φίλιππος 'fond of horses' (φίλος + ἵππος, the Macedonian royal name Philippos) and φιλάδελφος 'loving one's brother/sister' (φίλος + ἀδελφός), the epithet of Attalus II Philadelphus and Ptolemy II. The first item, 'philo-armonica', is NOT a Greek word: the ancestor of philharmonic is Italian filarmonico (from fil- 'phil-' + armonico, itself from Gk. (τὰ) ἁρμονικά 'theory of music'), which gave French philharmonique (1739) and English philharmonic (1813). Nourai's form is a Latino-Italian shape written as if Greek; the Greek elements are right but the compound is a modern one. Node verdict takes the worst of the three.
nodes.derivation_fa: از سه واژهٔ این جعبه، دو تای آخر ترکیب‌های اصیل یونانی‌اند: φίλιππος «اسب‌دوست» و φιλάδελφος «برادر‌دوست» (لقب آتالوس دوم و بطلمیوس دوم). اما philo-armonica واژه‌ای یونانی نیست؛ این ساخت از ایتالیایی filarmonico برآمده که خود از اجزای یونانی (philos + harmoniká) در دوران جدید ساخته شده است. بنابراین ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ دو واژه درست و دربارهٔ واژهٔ نخست با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

Watkins 1985 s.v. bhilo- lists only the phil- prefix words generally; it has no entry for a Greek compound *philarmonikos.

consulted.note: 'F. philharmonique, fr. It. filarmonico' — Italian is the intermediary.

'philharmonic, loving music. (Gk.) Gk. φίλ-ος, friendly, fond of; and L. -icus; Gk. ἁρμονία harmony' — Skeat too treats it as a modern coinage from Greek elements, with a Latin suffix, not as an inherited Greek compound.
The index line 'PHILADELPHIA … -PHILE bhilo- … PHILO- bhilo-' assigns the phil- words to the root; the -armonica part belongs under ar- (harmony), as Nourai's cross-reference ☞ Ar also says.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node with no refs in the book. It is right for two of the three words above: Latin took over Philippus and the Greek place-name Φιλαδέλφεια (the Lydian city of Revelation 3:7) as Philadelphia, and these Latin forms fed the modern languages. It is not the route of philharmonic, which reached French from Italian filarmonico without a Latin stage.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node: French has Philippe (from Latin Philippus), Philadelphie, and philharmonique, first recorded 1739 and borrowed from Italian filarmonico rather than from Latin. French is therefore a real link for Philippe/philharmonique and the donor of the Persian forms below, but for Philadelphia the English and Persian forms show the Latinate -ia, not French -ie.

nodes.words: (no transliterated word; script only: فیلارمونیک ، فیلیپ)
nodes.derivation: The two Persian forms in this box are 20th-century French loans: فیلارمونیک filārmonīk from French philharmonique (French -ique regularly gives Persian -یک, and French ph is heard as f, giving ف‌ی‌ل fil- for phil-), and فیلیپ Fīlīp from French Philippe (final -e is not pronounced, hence فیلیپ and not *فیلیپه). Both entered Persian through the French-mediated European vocabulary of the Qajar and Pahlavi periods, as the whole class of Persian musical and personal-name Gallicisms did.

nodes.derivation: philharmonic is exactly as drawn: English 1813, in the name of the London society, from French philharmonique (1739) < Italian filarmonico. Philip is Latin Philippus / Old French Philippe < Gk. Φίλιππος, so a French stage is defensible. Philadelphia is not from French: the Pennsylvania city was named by William Penn in 1682 straight from Greek φιλαδελφία 'brotherly love' (with the New-Testament Lydian city, named for Attalus II Philadelphus, in mind), and the English form keeps Greek/Latin -ia rather than French -ie. The node is therefore right in substance but its 'French' parent holds for only two of the three words.

nodes.derivation: Persian فیلادلفیا Fīlādelfīyā is the modern transcription of the American place-name, taken in its English/Latinate shape: the final -ia is rendered ـیا (as in ایتالیا، کالیفرنیا), which excludes a French Philadelphie as the model; ph is heard as f. Mo'in records such names in the aʿlām (proper-name) volumes, which is what the bare 'MON' citation points to.

nodes.derivation: No Greek *σῦς-φιλος is attested; the form is the modern back-explanation of the name Syphilus that Fracastoro gave his shepherd in 1530, and the elements are real Greek (ὗς/σῦς, gen. ὑός 'swine' + φίλος 'friend, loving'). Klein and Funk & Wagnalls both give exactly this analysis, so Nourai is following the standard 19th-20th c. dictionaries; but Etymonline notes that Fracastoro's intention is unknown and that the rival conjecture — an alteration of Sipylus, the son of Niobe in Ovid's Metamorphoses — is equally current. Hence plausible, not confirmed.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node, unreferenced in the book. It is right in that the coinage really is Latin — but New Latin of 1530, not ancient Latin: Girolamo Fracastoro of Verona wrote the hexameter poem Syphilis sive de morbo Gallico in Latin and there invented both the shepherd's name and, in his 1546 prose treatise De contagione, its use for the disease.

nodes.derivation: The gloss is accurate history: Fracastoro's 1530 poem, the shepherd Syphilus as the disease's first victim, the disease later named from the poem's hero. The language label is the weak point: the word is Modern/New Latin coined in Italy, not French; Klein, Etymonline and the AHD all say ModL/New Latin, and English syphilis is first recorded 1718. Nourai's 'French' is not baseless — Funk & Wagnalls (which he used elsewhere) marks English syphilis '[F.]', i.e. transmitted through French — so French is at most the vehicle to English, never the language of the coinage. One factual slip in the caption: Fracastoro's Syphilus is the FIRST VICTIM in the poem, not a real physician's patient, and it is the poem, not the hero, that gave the disease its name.
nodes.derivation_fa: متن توضیحی جعبه از نظر تاریخی درست است، اما برچسب زبانی آن نادرست است: واژه لاتینی نو (ModL) است که در ایتالیا ساخته شده، نه فرانسوی؛ کلاین و اتیمانلاین هر دو آن را ModL می‌دانند و نخستین کاربرد انگلیسی آن ۱۷۱۸ م. است. با این همه، فانک و واگنالز منشأ واژهٔ انگلیسی را «فرانسوی» می‌داند؛ پس فرانسه تنها واسطهٔ انتقال بوده است نه زبان سازندهٔ واژه.

nodes.derivation: Persian سیفیلیس sīfīlīs is the medical Gallicism of the Qajar/Pahlavi era, taken from French syphilis with the French pronunciation (final -s pronounced, hence ـس and not a silent ending); the doublet سفلیس seflīs is the colloquial reduction of the same word by loss of the unstressed first ī (sīfīlīs > seflīs), a very ordinary Persian shortening of long European words. Persian dictionaries define it purely as the disease.
nodes.derivation_fa: «سیفیلیس» وام‌واژه‌ای پزشکی از فرانسه (syphilis) است که در دوران قاجار و پهلوی به فارسی راه یافته و سِین پایانی آن مطابق تلفظ فرانسوی خوانده می‌شود. صورت دوم «سفلیس» گونهٔ کوتاه‌شدهٔ عامیانه است که از افتادن ای نخست پدید آمده (sīfīlīs > seflīs) — دگرگونی آوایی معمول در وام‌واژه‌های بلند اروپایی. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: philo-logos is correct: Greek φιλόλογος 'fond of discourse/learning', whence φιλολογία. But 'philo-anthôpos' is impossible: the Greek word is φιλάνθρωπος phil-ánthrōpos 'loving mankind' (φίλος + ἄνθρωπος 'man'), abstract φιλανθρωπία > Late Latin philanthropia > English philanthropy — the r of ἄνθρωπος is missing. I rendered PDF page 96 at 600 dpi and read the box: the printed page itself shows 'philo-anthôpos', so this is Nourai's own misprint and the JSON extraction is faithful. (Nourai's own cross-reference ☞ Ner 1 is to the root of ἀνήρ/ἄνθρωπος, which shows he meant ἄνθρωπος.)

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node, unreferenced. Latin borrowed both compounds as learned words: Late Latin philanthropia (in the Church Fathers, rendering Gk. φιλανθρωπία 'God's love of mankind') and classical Latin philologia (Cicero, of learned study; the title of Martianus Capella's De nuptiis Philologiae et Mercurii).
